source_text: Τοσοῦτον προαρπάζω τὴν εὐκοσμίαν, καὶ οὕτως οἰκειοῦ μαι τὰ κατορθώματα! Δʹ. Πᾶσι μὲν δὴ μάρτυσι πανηγυριστέον, καὶ πᾶσιν ἀνοικτέον ἑτοίμως καὶ γλῶσσαν, καὶ ἀκοὴν, καὶ διά νοιαν, καὶ λέγοντάς τι προθύμως περὶ αὐτῶν καὶ ἀκούοντας, καὶ πάντα ἐλάττω νομίζοντας τῆς ἐκεί νων ἀθλήσεως. Καὶ γὰρ οὕτως ἔχει, πολλῶν ὄντων ἡμῖν εἰς ὁδηγίαν τοῦ κρείττονος, καὶ πολλῶν τῶν πρὸς ἀρετὴν παιδευμάτων, λόγου, νόμου, προφητῶν, ἀποστόλων, αὐτῶν τῶν Χριστοῦ παθημάτων, τοῦ πρώτου μάρτυρος ἐπὶ τὸν σταυρὸν ἀνελθόντος, κἀμὲ συναγαγόντος, ἵνα προσηλώσῃ τὴν ἐμὴν ἁμαρτίαν, καὶ τὸν ὄφιν θριαμβεύσῃ, καὶ τὸ ξύλον ἁγιάσῃ, καὶ τὴν ἡδονὴν νικήσῃ, καὶ τὸν Ἀδὰμ ἀνα σώσῃ, καὶ τὴν εἰκόνα πεσοῦσαν ἀνακαλέσηται· τοσ ούτων ὄντων ἡμῖν καὶ τοιούτων, οὐδὲν ἔλαττον ἡμῖν εἰς παιδαγωγίαν οἱ μάρτυρες, ὁλοκαυτώματα λογικὰ, θύματα τέλεια, προσφοραὶ δεκταὶ, τῆς ἀλη θείας κηρύγματα, τοῦ ψεύδους στηλιτεύματα, νόμου συμπλήρωσις, τοῦ γε πνευματικῶς νοουμένου, πλάνης κατάλυσις, κακίας διωγμὸς, ἁμαρτίας κατακλυσμὸς, κόσμου καθάρσιον. Εʹ. Σὺ δέ μοι, Κυπριανὲ, τὸ τιμιώτατόν μοι καὶ πρᾶγμα καὶ ὄνομα, πλέον ἢ κατὰ τοὺς ἄλλους μάρτυρας (φθόνος γὰρ οὐδεὶς παρὰ μαρτύρων μάρτυσιν)· καὶ σοῦ διαφερόντως ἥττημαί τε τῆς ἀρετῆς, καὶ τῇ μνήμῃ κουφίζομαι, καὶ ὥσπερ ἔνθους ὑφ' ἡδονῆς γίνομαι, καί τινα τρόπον σύνειμί τε τῇ μαρτυρίᾳ, καὶ κοινωνῶ τῆς ἀθλήσεως, καὶ ὅλος πρὸς σὲ μετανίσταμαι· τάχα μὲν διὰ τὴν τῶν λόγων οἰκείωσιν, οἷς τοσοῦτον τῶν ἄλλων ἐκράτεις, ὅσον τὰ λογικὰ τῆς ἀλόγου φύσεως (συνεισέρχεται γὰρ, οὐκ οἶδ' ὅπως, φίλτρον τοῖς κατά τι συναπτομένοις, οὐχ ἧττον τοῖς λοιποῖς πράγμασιν, ἢ τοῖς περὶ ἀγχιστείαν αἵματος)· τάχα δὲ διὰ τὸ τῆς μεταβολῆς ἀθρόον τε καὶ παρά δοξον, ὃ κρεῖττον λόγου καὶ παραδείγματος. Ἐπεὶ γλυκὺ μὲν ἥλιος μετὰ νέφος, ᾧ τέως συνεκαλύπτετο· γλύκιον δὲ τὸ ἔαρ, ὅτι μετὰ χειμῶνος κατ ήφειαν· ἡδίων δὲ μειδιῶσα γαλήνη, καὶ θάλασσα ἡπλωμένη, καὶ ταῖς ἀκταῖς προσπαίζουσα μετὰ πνευμάτων στάσιν, καὶ ὠδίνοντα κύματα. ςʹ. Οὗτος Κυπριανὸς, ὦ ἄνδρες (ἵνα οἱ μὲν εἰδότες, ἡδίους γένησθε τῇ ὑπομνήσει, οἱ δὲ ἀγνοοῦντες, μάθητε τὸ κάλλιστον τῶν ἡμετέρων διηγημάτων, καὶ τὴν κοινὴν Χριστιανῶν φιλοτιμίαν), οὗτος ἐκεῖνος, τὸ μέγα ποτὲ Καρχηδονίων ὄνομα, νῦν δὲ τῆς οἰκουμέ νης ἁπάσης, ὁ πλούτῳ περιφανὴς, καὶ δυναστείᾳ περίβλεπτος, καὶ γένει γνώριμος (εἴ γε μέγιστον εἰς εὐγενείας ἀπόδειξιν, συγκλήτου βουλῆς μετουσία καὶ προεδρία), τὸ τῆς νεότητος ἄνθος, τὸ τῆς φύσεως ἄγαλμα, τὸ τῶν λόγων κράτος, τῶν τε κατὰ φιλοσοφίαν, καὶ ὅσοι τῆς ἄλλης παιδεύσεως, καὶ τού των ὃ βούλει μέρος· ὡς μᾶλλον μὲν τὸ ποικίλον ἢ τὸ ἄκρον ἐν ἑκάστῳ θαυμάζεσθαι, μᾶλλον δὲ τὸ εὐδόκιμον ἐν ἑκάστῳ τῆς περὶ πάντα πολυμαθίας· ἢ, ἵνα διέλω σαφέστερον, τῶν μὲν τῷ ποικίλῳ, τῶν δὲ τῷ ἄκρῳ, ἔστι δὲ ὧν ἀμφοτέροις, πᾶσι δὲ πάντων ἐκράτει. Ζʹ. Τῶν μὲν οὖν λόγων καὶ οἱ λόγοι μάρτυρες, οὓς πολλοὺς καὶ λαμπροὺς ἐκεῖνος ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν κατε βάλετο, ἐπειδή γε μετήνεγκε Θεοῦ φιλανθρωπίᾳ τὴν παίδευσιν, τοῦ ποιοῦντος τὰ πάντα καὶ μετασκευάζοντος, πρὸς τὸ βέλτιον, καὶ τῷ λόγῳ τὴν ἀλο γίαν ὑπέκλινεν· τὸ δὲ ἐντεῦθεν, οὐκ οἶδ' ὅπως χρή σωμαι, τῷ λόγῳ καὶ τίς γένωμαι· πῶς μὲν μὴ μακρὸν ἀποτείνω λόγον, καὶ παντελῶς ἔξω τοῦ και ροῦ, πάντων τῶν Κυπριανοῦ μεμνημένος· πῶς δὲ μὴ τὰ μέγιστα ζημιώσω τοὺς παρόντας τοῖς σιωπωμένοις.
thought_title: All martyrs must be honored, Cyprian most of all
orientation: Gregory addresses his congregation to praise all martyrs as teachers and then singles out Cyprian for his learning and sudden conversion.
pass_a_gloss: So greatly do I seize beforehand the good order, and so do I make my own the successes! For all martyrs a festival must be kept, and for all men tongue and hearing and thought must be opened readily, both while speaking something eagerly about them and while listening, and while counting all things less than their contest. For so it is: though there are many things to us for guidance to the better, and many trainings toward virtue — speech, law, prophets, apostles, the very sufferings of Christ, who as the first martyr went up upon the cross, and gathered me together with himself, in order that he might nail up my sin, and might triumph over the serpent, and might sanctify the wood, and might conquer pleasure, and might save Adam, and might call back the fallen image — though so many and such things are to us, the martyrs are nothing less to us for instruction: reasonable sacrifices, perfect victims, acceptable offerings, proclamations of the truth, public shaming of falsehood, fulfillment of the law, at least of the law understood spiritually, dissolution of error, pursuit of evil, flood of sin, purification of the world. But you to me, Cyprian, most honored to me both as deed and as name, more than the other martyrs — for there is no envy from martyrs toward martyrs — and by you especially I both have been defeated by your virtue, and am lightened by your memory, and as if possessed I become through pleasure, and in a certain manner I am both present together with the martyrdom, and I share in the contest, and wholly I remove over to you; perhaps on the one hand because of the kinship of words, by which you held so much beyond the others, as much as rational things hold beyond irrational nature — for there enters, I know not how, affection for those joined together in something, not less in other matters than in matters of kinship of blood — but perhaps on the other hand because of the sudden and unexpected character of the change, which is beyond speech and example. For sweet is sun after cloud, by which for a while it was covered; and spring is sweeter, because it comes after the gloom of winter; and more pleasant is smiling calm, and sea spread flat, and playing with the shores after ceasing of winds and laboring waves. This is Cyprian, O men — in order that you who know may become sweeter by the reminder, and you who are ignorant may learn the most beautiful of our narratives, and the common love of honor of Christians — this is that man, once the great name of the Carthaginians, but now of the whole inhabited world, the one conspicuous by wealth, and looked to because of power, and known by birth — if indeed participation and presidency of the senatorial council is the greatest proof of nobility — the flower of youth, the statue of nature, the power of words, both those according to philosophy and as many as belong to the other education, and of these whatever part you wish; so that rather the varied than the highest in each thing is wondered at, but rather the approved reputation in each thing than the much-learning concerning all; or, that I may divide more clearly, over some by the varied, over others by the highest, and there are some by both, but over all men he held over all things. Of his words, then, even his words are witnesses, which being many and brilliant he laid down on our behalf, since by the love of God for mankind He transferred his education — He who makes all things and refashions them toward the better — and by the word He made irrationality yield; but from here on, I know not how I should use speech and what I should become: how on the one hand I should not stretch out a long speech, and one altogether outside the occasion, remembering all the things of Cyprian; and how on the other hand I should not deprive those present of the greatest things by the things passed over in silence.

choices.why: masculine singular noun for a person, identified as Christ who went up on the cross
brief glossary term ὁλοκαύτωμα must be sacrifice
brief glossary term ἄθλησις must be contest

choices.english: by the love of God for mankind He transferred his education
choices.why: verb is 3rd singular with God as implied subject and dative of means; Cyprian is object of transfer, not subject

choices.english: by the word He made irrationality yield
choices.why: same divine subject continues; ἀλογία is irrational condition, not doctrine
rejected: he made unreason yield to the Word

pass_b_english: This is how eagerly I seize their good order in advance, and how fully I make their triumphs my own! Every martyr deserves our festival, and for every martyr we should readily open tongue and ear and mind, speaking eagerly about them and listening, and counting everything less than their contest.

That is how it truly stands. We have many guides toward what is better, and many schools of training in virtue: speech, the Law, the prophets, the apostles, and the sufferings of Christ himself, the first martyr, who went up upon the cross and gathered me with him, so that he might nail my sin to it (Colossians 2:14), and triumph over the serpent (Colossians 2:15), and sanctify the wood, and conquer pleasure, and save Adam, and call back the fallen image. With guides so many and so great, the martyrs still teach us no less. They are reasonable sacrifices, perfect victims, acceptable offerings, proclamations of the truth, public shaming of falsehood, the fulfillment of the Law, at least of the Law understood spiritually, the overthrow of error, the driving out of evil, a flood against sin, and the cleansing of the world.

But you, Cyprian, mean more to me than any other, in both deed and name — more than the other martyrs, although martyrs feel no envy toward martyrs. Your virtue has conquered me in a special way, and I am lifted by your memory, and I become almost inspired with joy, and in a sense I stand beside your witness, and I share in your contest, and I pass over wholly to you. Perhaps this comes from our kinship in words, in which you surpassed other men as much as rational beings surpass an irrational nature — for somehow, I know not how, affection steals in among those joined by anything at all, no less in other pursuits than in closeness of blood. Perhaps it comes from the sudden and astonishing character of your conversion, which is beyond speech and example. For the sun is sweet after the cloud that had hidden it, and spring is sweeter still because it comes after the gloom of winter, and a smiling calm is lovelier, and the sea spread flat and playing against the shore, after the winds have ceased and the waves have ceased laboring.

This Cyprian, gentlemen — so that those who know may find remembrance sweeter, and those who do not know may learn the finest of our stories and the common pride of Christians — this is that man, once the great name of Carthage and now of the whole world, conspicuous for wealth, distinguished for power, and notable for birth, if sharing and presiding in the senate is the greatest proof of nobility. He was the flower of youth, the image of nature, and a power in words, both in philosophy and in every other kind of education, and in whatever branch of them you choose. In each field, people admired variety more than mastery, or rather they admired his distinction in each field more than his breadth of learning in all. To put it more plainly, he surpassed some by variety, others by mastery, and still others by both, but he surpassed all men in all things.

His own discourses witness to his eloquence, the many brilliant works he laid down on our behalf, since he transferred his education, by the love for mankind of God, who makes all things and refashions them toward the better, and he bowed irrationality before the Word. From here on I do not know how to use speech or what to become: how to avoid spinning out a long speech, wholly out of season, if I recall everything in Cyprian, and how to avoid cheating those present of the greatest things by what I leave unsaid.
notes: Source has broken spacing and line-break artifacts, e.g. ἐκεί νων, Ἀδὰμ ἀνα σῳσῃ, οἰκουμέ νης, but sense is recoverable; gloss follows restored words without inventing text.

problems.quote: once God in His love for mankind transferred his education
problems.source_quote: ἐπειδή γε μετήνεγκε Θεοῦ φιλανθρωπίᾳ τὴν παίδευσιν
problems.why: The subject of μετήνεγκε is Cyprian, who transferred his education. God's love for mankind is the means, not the agent. The English makes God the one who transfers it.
problems.fix: since he transferred his education, by the love for mankind of God, who makes all things and refashions them toward the better,

problems.quote: His own words witness to his words
problems.source_quote: Τῶν μὲν οὖν λόγων καὶ οἱ λόγοι μάρτυρες
problems.why: His discourses witness to his eloquence; the English repeats 'words' and loses that distinction.
problems.fix: His own discourses are the witnesses of his eloquence
problems.ruling: Τῶν λόγων καὶ οἱ λόγοι μάρτυρες: 'words' = eloquence/discourse, then his works/orations witness. 'His own words witness to his words' obscures the distinction and misleads.

problems.quote: and by His Word made its irrationality yield
problems.source_quote: καὶ τῷ λόγῳ τὴν ἀλογίαν ὑπέκλινεν
problems.why: Cyprian is the subject: he made irrationality bow to the Word. The English gives this to God, and 'its' has no clear referent.
problems.fix: and bowed irrationality before the Word.
problems.ruling: Cyprian, subject of μετήνεγκε, still governs ὑπέκλινεν: he bowed τὴν ἀλογίαν to τῷ λόγῳ. English makes God the agent, and 'its' is unanchored.

fixed: agency transfer: fixed — μετήνεγκε has Cyprian as subject and Θεοῦ φιλανθρωπίᾳ is means, so God is not the transferrer

last_rejected.quote: he transferred his education, by the love for mankind of God, who makes all things and refashions them toward the better
last_rejected.source_quote: μετήνεγκε Θεοῦ φιλανθρωπίᾳ τὴν παίδευσιν, τοῦ ποιοῦντος τὰ πάντα καὶ μετασκευάζοντος, πρὸς τὸ βέλτιον
last_rejected.why: πρὸς τὸ βέλτιον is the goal of Cyprian’s transfer of education; English assigns it to God’s refashioning.
last_rejected.fix: By the love for mankind of God, who makes and refashions all things, he turned his education toward the better.
last_rejected.ruling: πρὸς τὸ βέλτιον follows τοῦ ποιοῦντος τὰ πάντα καὶ μετασκευάζοντος, so God's refashioning toward the better is the natural reading. The English is acceptable.
